title: 7Q10
summary: The lowest 7-consecutive-day average streamflow expected on average once every ten years — the design low flow for sizing effluent dilution.
body:
The **7Q10** is a low-flow statistic: the lowest average streamflow over any
seven consecutive days that, statistically, recurs about once every ten years. It
is the conventional *design low flow* in NPDES permitting — the worst-case
dilution condition a discharge must meet water-quality criteria under.

Because it represents the stream at its weakest, the 7Q10 is the denominator in an
[[assimilative capacity]] screen: the lower the design flow, the less clean water
is available to dilute a pollutant load or to absorb a reduction in flow from
[[consumptive cooling]]. In the analysis the receiving water's 7Q10 is read from
the NPDES permit fact sheet stream-flows table, not estimated.

title: AEP
summary: The investor-owned utility whose Ohio operating company serves much of the grid footprint in this record.
body:
**American Electric Power** is one of the largest electric utilities in the United
States; its Ohio operating company, AEP Ohio, is the distribution utility across much
of the territory this record covers. As a regulated utility it delivers power under
rates and terms set by the [[PUCO]], and its transmission sits inside the [[PJM]]
market.

AEP is a recurring named party in the data-center story because it is the utility that
must actually serve the new load — building substations, negotiating special
arrangements for hyperscale customers, and forecasting the demand growth those
customers drive. Its filings at the PUCO and its role in [[PJM]] planning are where the
utility's own account of a project's power needs appears, to be read against the
neutral baseline of the [[EIA]] utility data.

title: Assimilative capacity
summary: A stream's ability to dilute or assimilate an added load (or a loss of flow) without breaching water-quality criteria, evaluated at design low flow.
body:
**Assimilative capacity** is the headroom a receiving water has to absorb a
pollutant load — or a withdrawal of flow — before a water-quality criterion would
be exceeded. It is evaluated at a design low flow, conventionally the
[[7Q10]], so the screen reflects the stream when it is least able to dilute.

In the water-balance analysis, the campus's [[consumptive cooling]] draw is
subtracted from the live receiving-water flow and compared against the 7Q10: a
negative balance means the consumptive loss erodes the dilution flow the permit
record assumes, shrinking assimilative headroom. A negative figure is a screening
flag — a lead to verify against the live gauge and the permit, not a verdict.

title: Behind-the-meter
summary: On-site generation that serves a load directly, without that power crossing the utility meter or the public grid.
body:
**Behind-the-meter** generation sits on the customer's side of the utility meter and
feeds its load directly — gas turbines, engines, fuel cells, or solar paired with
storage. In a self-supply, non-export configuration that power need never cross the
meter onto the public grid; many BTM assets, though, stay grid-connected for backup
or to export surplus, which pulls them back under the utility's and market's rules.
The arrangement lets a large user self-supply some or all of its demand rather than
draw it entirely from the utility.

For a [[hyperscale data center]], behind-the-meter generation is a way around the
grid's constraints: it can bring a campus online without waiting out the
[[interconnection queue]] or funding the transmission upgrades a full grid connection
would require. But it moves the impact rather than removing it — on-site combustion
becomes an air-permitting question (a [[permit to install]]), and a "behind-the-meter"
plant that also leans on the grid for backup still shows up in [[PJM]]'s planning. The
platform treats a claimed behind-the-meter design as a sourced assumption to verify,
because it changes both the emissions and the grid-cost story.

title: Brownfield
summary: A property whose redevelopment is complicated by real or perceived contamination, often carrying cleanup obligations and dedicated funding.
body:
A **brownfield** is a property — usually a former industrial or commercial site —
whose reuse is complicated by the presence, or the suspicion, of contamination. The
label is regulatory shorthand that unlocks assessment and cleanup programs and
dedicated grants, on the theory that redeveloping an already-disturbed site is
preferable to consuming greenfield land.

A brownfield sits at the seam of the environmental and land-use threads. Its
contamination history may tie to a formal [[CERCLA]] liability or to a lesser state
cleanup, and its redevelopment is frequently sweetened with a [[tax abatement]] on top
of remediation funding. For a facility record, the brownfield designation is both a
constraint and a lead: it flags residual contamination that governs what can be built
and how, and it points back to the site's prior uses and the parties responsible for
them.

title: CERCLA
aliases: Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act
summary: The federal Superfund statute governing the cleanup of contaminated sites and the strict, retroactive liability of the parties responsible for them.
body:
**CERCLA** — the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act,
better known as Superfund — is the federal law for cleaning up releases of hazardous
substances. Its defining feature is liability: it imposes strict and retroactive
responsibility on the parties connected to a site — joint and several where the harm
is indivisible, though a party that proves a divisible share can be apportioned only
that much — so cleanup costs can attach to owners and operators long after the
contamination occurred.

CERCLA anchors the most serious contamination in the record. A site on the National
Priorities List carries a formal cleanup and, for a federal installation, a
[[federal facility agreement]] setting the schedule. The statute is also expanding —
the designation of certain [[PFAS]] as hazardous substances pulls those compounds into
its liability scheme. Where a contaminated property is being redeveloped rather than
listed, it usually appears instead as a [[brownfield]], the lighter-touch cousin of a
Superfund cleanup.

title: CGP
summary: The NPDES general permit that authorizes stormwater discharges from construction sites disturbing an acre or more — including smaller sites within a common plan of development or sale that reaches an acre — under a standard set of conditions.
body:
A **construction general permit** is the [[NPDES]] mechanism for stormwater running
off a construction site. Rather than issue an individual permit to every project, the
regulator writes one general permit and a site enrolls under it by filing a notice of
intent and a stormwater pollution prevention plan. It applies to construction
disturbing an acre or more — the threshold most large campus builds clear easily.

The CGP is the earliest water-side paper trail of a project's *construction* phase,
distinct from the operating [[NPDES]] permit that governs the finished facility. Its
enrollment names the operator, the acreage disturbed, and the receiving water, and it
obligates the [[erosion and sediment control]] practices that keep bare-soil runoff —
amplified by the site's soils and [[curve number]] — out of the stream during the
build. For the platform, a CGP filing is often the first hard confirmation that a
proposed data-center site is actually moving dirt.

title: Closed-loop cooling
summary: A recirculating cooling design whose water loss is chiefly evaporation and blowdown, so it withdraws little but consumes most of what it takes.
body:
**Closed-loop cooling** recirculates its cooling water rather than returning it to
the source. The system loses water two ways — evaporation from the cooling tower, and
periodic *blowdown* to purge concentrated minerals — and makes up the difference with
fresh withdrawal. The result inverts the once-through profile: a modest withdrawal
but a high consumptive fraction.

For a [[hyperscale data center]] this is the design that matters to the river,
because most of what it withdraws is lost to evaporation and never returns
downstream — the [[consumptive cooling]] that is subtracted from live flow in the
[[dilution]] and [[assimilative capacity]] screen. It also concentrates whatever is
in the make-up water, so blowdown itself can become a permitted discharge. A
recirculating design cuts the withdrawal an [[once-through cooling]] plant would need
while raising the share that leaves the watershed for good.

title: CMAR
summary: A project-delivery method in which the construction manager joins during design and commits to a guaranteed maximum price for the build.
body:
**Construction manager at risk** is a delivery method in which the owner hires a
construction manager early, during design, to advise on cost and constructability, and
the CM then commits to a *guaranteed maximum price* to build the project. The "at risk"
is literal: overruns above the GMP are the manager's exposure, not the owner's, which
aligns the CM with holding the budget.

CMAR matters to the platform because it shapes the cost record. Under this method the
early [[opinion of probable cost]] and the later GMP are the checkpoints where a public
project's price is set and can be reconstructed, and the CM is usually selected through
a qualifications-based [[request for qualifications]] rather than low bid. Knowing a
project used CMAR tells the analyst which documents carry the authoritative numbers and
how the contractor was chosen.

title: Colocation
summary: A data center that leases space, power, and cooling to multiple tenants who install their own hardware — distinct from a single operator's owned campus.
body:
**Colocation** is the data-center model in which the facility operator sells space,
power, and cooling by the rack, cage, or suite to multiple tenants who bring their own
servers. The colo provider owns the building and the infrastructure; the customers own
the computing. It contrasts with an owner-operated campus, where a single company like
a [[hyperscaler]] builds and runs the whole facility for its own workloads.

The distinction shapes who is accountable in the record. A [[hyperscale data center]]
has one identifiable operator behind its water and power footprint; a colocation
facility diffuses that across a shifting set of tenants who may be undisclosed, which
complicates tracing the end user of a given load. Some colos also accredit to secure
tiers like [[IL6]] to host government tenants — another reason the tenant behind a
colo's capacity can be harder to pin down than its operator.

title: Common-control plumbing
summary: Shared registered agents, organizers, or addresses across entities — evidence of common administrative control, not of beneficial ownership.
body:
**Common-control plumbing** is the term this project uses for the administrative
overlaps that recur across the entity record: a shared registered agent, the same
organizer or counsel, a reused mailing address. Those overlaps are evidence that
entities are *administered together* — the plumbing of common control — and are
useful for resolving who is really one actor in the entity graph.

They are deliberately **not** statements about beneficial ownership. Per the
site's evidence discipline, such links are tagged `[inference]` (a labelled
reading of the record), and the graph's roles and edges are leads to verify, not
verdicts. The distinction matters most where the plumbing connects the entities
assembling a [[hyperscale data center]] campus.

title: Conditional use
summary: A use allowed in a zoning district only by case-by-case approval, granted with conditions rather than by right.
body:
A **conditional use** is a use the zoning code lists as permissible in a district but
only with discretionary approval — the applicant must show it meets standards and
accept conditions attached to it. It is decided administratively or by a zoning board,
not by the legislature, which distinguishes it from a [[rezoning]]: the underlying
district does not change, the use is simply cleared within it.

The conditional-use path lets a project avoid a full rezoning fight when its zoning
already contemplates the use, trading a legislative vote for negotiated conditions —
buffers, hours, traffic or utility commitments. For the record, the value is in those
conditions: they are where a community extracts concrete obligations from a
data-center or industrial user, and where a later dispute over compliance is
anchored. A conditional use is a narrower instrument than a [[variance]], which waives
a standard rather than authorizing a listed use.

title: Consent decree
summary: A court-approved settlement in which a party agrees to specified actions under continuing judicial oversight, carrying the force of a court order.
body:
A **consent decree** is a settlement that a court adopts as its own order. Rather than
litigate to judgment, the parties negotiate terms — often injunctive steps, a
compliance schedule, and penalties — and the court enters them, so the agreement
becomes judicially enforceable and stays under the court's supervision until its
obligations are met.

In the environmental record the consent decree is the usual endpoint of a serious
enforcement track: a discharger in [[significant non-compliance]], or a party liable
under [[CERCLA]], resolves the matter by agreeing to a decree that fixes what it must
do and by when. Because it is a public court document, a consent decree is a
high-value, [verified] source — it states the violations conceded, the remedy imposed,
and the deadlines that follow, and it often surfaces in [[ECHO]] as the formal action
that closed out a compliance case.

title: Constructive denial
summary: An agency's failure to produce public records within a reasonable time, treated in law as a denial even though no formal refusal was issued.
body:
**Constructive denial** is the doctrine that an agency can deny a public-records
request without ever saying no. Under Ohio's Public Records Act (R.C. 149.43), records
must be produced within a *reasonable* time; when an agency instead lets a request sit,
runs out the clock, or answers with open-ended delay, the law can treat that silence as
a denial the requester may act on.

The concept matters because it closes an obvious loophole: if only an explicit refusal
were reviewable, an agency could defeat transparency simply by not responding.
Constructive denial gives the requester a ripened claim — the predicate for a
[[public-records mandamus]] action to compel production. In this record, where the
requester seeks documents an agency is slow to release, the timing and content of the
agency's non-response is what establishes whether a denial has constructively occurred
under the [[Ohio Revised Code]].

title: Consumptive cooling
summary: Cooling water that is withdrawn and lost (mostly to evaporation) rather than returned to the source, reducing downstream flow.
body:
**Consumptive cooling** is the share of a facility's cooling-water withdrawal that
does not return to the watercourse — primarily evaporative loss from cooling
towers. Unlike a once-through return, a consumptive draw permanently removes flow
from the system downstream of the intake.

For a [[hyperscale data center]], the consumptive fraction of the cooling demand
is the quantity that matters to the river: it is subtracted from live flow in the
[[assimilative capacity]] screen against the [[7Q10]]. The water-balance model
treats the cooling demand and its consumptive fraction as scenario inputs
(labelled assumptions), while the receiving-water flows are read from live gauges
and the permit record.

Whether the rejected heat is dumped or recovered is a separate design axis —
see [[heat reuse]] — that can shift the consumptive fraction where recovery
displaces evaporative rejection.

title: CRA
summary: An Ohio property-tax-abatement district (R.C. 3735) that lets a municipality exempt the value of new construction to incentivize development.
body:
A **community reinvestment area** is an Ohio economic-development tool under R.C.
3735: a local government designates an area where new construction and improvements
can receive a partial or total exemption from real-property taxes for a set term. It
is one of the state's most-used [[tax abatement]] vehicles, and for a large project
the abatement is usually memorialized in a negotiated agreement with job and
investment commitments.

The CRA is central to the data-center financing thread because it is how the abated
value is delivered: a campus worth hundreds of millions can have most of that value
exempted for a decade or more, shifting the visible public benefit from property tax
to a negotiated [[payment in lieu of taxes]] or a school-district revenue-share.
Reading a CRA agreement — its term, its exemption percentage, and what the developer
promised in return — is how the platform tests whether a deal's public benefit
matches its public cost.

title: Curve number
summary: The NRCS coefficient (0–100) relating land cover and soil to the depth of runoff a storm produces — the core parameter of the curve-number runoff method.
body:
The **runoff curve number** is a single coefficient between 0 and 100 that captures
how much of a rainfall a piece of land turns into runoff. A low CN (forest on sandy
[[HSG]] A soil) absorbs most of a storm; a high CN (pavement, or clay HSG D soil)
sheds nearly all of it. The NRCS method looks the number up from a land-cover ×
soil-group table.

Curve number is where land-use change becomes hydrology. Converting cropland or
woods to the roofs and parking of a large campus raises the site CN, so the same
storm yields more runoff, faster — the effect a post-construction stormwater design
and its [[erosion and sediment control]] have to hold. Because the output is
sensitive to the CN, a small error in the assumed soil group or cover class
propagates straight into the modeled peak flow.

title: Dilution
summary: The clean receiving-water flow available to dilute a discharged load, sized at design low flow — the physical basis of a water-quality-based effluent limit.
body:
**Dilution** is the mixing of a discharged pollutant load into the clean flow of the
receiving water. Because a stream is weakest at low flow, water-quality-based
[[effluent]] limits are sized against the design low flow — the [[7Q10]] — so the
discharge still meets criteria under the worst realistic dilution. Regulators may
recognize a bounded *mixing zone* immediately downstream of an outfall where
criteria are allowed to be met at the zone's edge rather than the pipe.

Dilution is the hinge between the water-quality thread and the data-center thread of
this record. A large [[consumptive cooling]] withdrawal removes flow from the same
reach that dilutes a downstream discharge, so it shrinks the [[assimilative capacity]]
available to every permitted load below the intake — a coupling the water-balance
model makes explicit rather than assuming away.

title: Dissolved oxygen
summary: The oxygen dissolved in water and available to aquatic life; a core water-quality criterion that a discharge must not depress below standard.
body:
**Dissolved oxygen** is the concentration of oxygen dissolved in water, the supply
that fish and aquatic insects breathe. It is a foundational water-quality criterion:
a stream must hold dissolved oxygen above a numeric floor, and an [[NPDES]] permit's
[[effluent]] limits are set partly to protect it.

Dissolved oxygen is where several loads converge. Oxygen-demanding organic matter
and ammonia in a discharge consume it directly; nutrient loading consumes it
indirectly, because the algal blooms that [[total phosphorus]] and
[[total nitrogen]] feed die and decay, drawing the reach down into an oxygen sag.
Low flow makes all of this worse — less water holds less oxygen and dilutes less
load — which is why a discharge's oxygen impact is judged at the same design low
flow as its [[dilution]].

title: DMR
summary: The self-reported effluent-monitoring data a permittee files with the regulator, the primary public record of whether a discharge meets its permit.
body:
A **discharge monitoring report** is the periodic (usually monthly) filing in which
an [[NPDES]] permittee reports its measured [[effluent]] — flow, concentrations, and
loads — against each permit limit. It is a self-report, but a federally enforceable
one: a false or omitted DMR is itself a violation.

The DMR is the workhorse record of water compliance. Because the reports are public
and machine-readable through EPA's [[ECHO]], they let an outside analyst reconstruct
a facility's compliance history without a records request — recurring exceedances
are what tip a permittee into [[significant non-compliance]]. For the platform they
are a source of *reported* quantities: a DMR value is [verified] as filed, while any
figure derived from it (a load trend, an annual mass) is an [inference] built on top.

title: ECHO
summary: EPA's public database of facility permits, inspections, violations, and enforcement actions across its major programs.
body:
**Enforcement and Compliance History Online** is the [[EPA]] portal that consolidates
a facility's regulatory record — its permits, inspections, reported violations, and
formal enforcement — across the water, air, and waste programs. It ingests the
self-reported [[discharge monitoring report]] data and surfaces derived flags like
[[significant non-compliance]], all keyed to a facility identifier.

ECHO is the platform's workhorse for facility compliance because it is public,
queryable, and national — an outside analyst can reconstruct a discharger's history
without a records request. Its data seeds several of the platform's reference
datasets, including the [[NPDES]] inventory and the facility list behind the [[RSEI]]
risk screen. An ECHO record is [reference] as pulled; the platform dates and caches it
so a compliance claim stays anchored to the snapshot it was drawn from.

title: Effluent
summary: Treated wastewater discharged to a receiving water; its pollutant concentrations and loads are capped by limits written into the NPDES permit.
body:
**Effluent** is the treated water a facility discharges to a stream, river, or
lake. Its permitted *effluent limits* — numeric caps on concentration and mass load
for each regulated pollutant — are the operative terms of an [[NPDES]] permit, and
the permittee proves compliance by reporting measured effluent quality in the
monthly [[discharge monitoring report]].

Effluent limits are set two ways, and the stricter governs: technology-based limits
reflect what treatment can achieve, while water-quality-based limits protect the
receiving water given its [[dilution]] at design low flow. That second path is why a
[[WWTP]] discharge to a small stream can carry tighter limits than the same plant on
a large river — the same [[assimilative capacity]] logic that a new
[[consumptive cooling]] draw erodes by removing dilution flow.

title: EIA
summary: The federal statistical agency for U.S. energy production, consumption, and prices, and a primary source of utility-level demand data.
body:
The **Energy Information Administration** is the independent statistical arm of the
U.S. Department of Energy. It publishes the authoritative public numbers on energy —
generation, fuel mix, prices, and, through survey forms like EIA-861, the sales and
customer counts of individual electric utilities.

EIA data is the platform's neutral baseline for the energy backdrop of a site: it
establishes a utility's existing load and customer base as [reference] facts, against
which the *demand pressure* of a new hyperscale campus can be measured. Because it is
survey-based and utility-level, EIA is how an outside analyst estimates what share of
a utility's growth a single data center represents — a framing that a company like
[[AEP]] or the [[PJM]] load forecast can then corroborate or complicate.

title: Enterprise zone
summary: An Ohio program that grants property-tax exemptions on new investment in a designated area in exchange for job-creation and investment commitments.
body:
An **enterprise zone** is an Ohio economic-development program in which a local
government designates an area and offers real- and personal-property tax exemptions
to firms that invest and create jobs there. The deal is struck in an *enterprise zone
agreement* that sets the exemption percentage and term against specific, enforceable
commitments — dollars invested, jobs created and retained, payroll thresholds.

The enterprise zone sits alongside the [[community reinvestment area]] as one of
Ohio's two main [[tax abatement]] frameworks; which one a project uses turns on
statutory eligibility and local practice. What makes the enterprise-zone agreement
useful to the record is its *clawback* structure: because the exemption is tied to
performance promises, the agreement states what the developer owes if the jobs or
investment fail to materialize — a test a capital-intensive but low-headcount data
center frequently strains.

title: EPA
summary: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency — the federal environmental regulator that sets national standards and delegates much of their enforcement to states.
body:
The **U.S. Environmental Protection Agency** is the federal environmental regulator.
It writes the national rules under statutes like the Clean Water Act and CERCLA, runs
the public data systems the platform relies on — [[ECHO]], the [[TRI]], and the
[[RSEI]] model built on it — and retains direct authority over federal programs and
facilities.

Much of the day-to-day permitting and enforcement, though, is *delegated*: the EPA
sets the floor and a state agency like the [[Ohio EPA]] issues the permits and brings
most of the cases. That division is why a facility's record usually has both a federal
and a state layer, and why the platform reads EPA data as the neutral national
baseline while treating a state agency's actions as the operative local decisions.

title: ESC
summary: The construction practices that keep disturbed soil and sediment out of stormwater and receiving waters while a site is being built.
body:
**Erosion and sediment control** is the set of temporary practices — silt fence,
sediment basins, stabilized entrances, cover on bare ground — that a construction
site uses to keep loosened soil from washing into storm drains and streams. Sediment
is itself a regulated pollutant, and it carries phosphorus and other contaminants
with it, so controlling it protects downstream water quality during the build.

ESC is the operative content of a site's stormwater plan under its
[[construction general permit]]. Its demands scale with the site: erodible soils, the
lower-infiltration [[HSG]] classes (C and D), and steeper slopes raise the
[[curve number]] and shed more sediment-laden runoff, so they need more control. On a multi-hundred-acre data-center clearing, the adequacy and
upkeep of erosion and sediment control is a recurring compliance question — and a
lapse in it is a common early violation in the construction record.

title: FERC
summary: The federal regulator of interstate electricity transmission, wholesale power markets, and the RTOs that operate them.
body:
The **Federal Energy Regulatory Commission** is the federal agency that regulates
interstate transmission and wholesale electricity markets. It approves the tariffs and
market rules that a [[regional transmission organization]] like [[PJM]] operates
under, including the interconnection process and the capacity market that shape how new
load and generation are accommodated.

FERC sits at the top of the grid's three-tier oversight in this record: it governs the
wholesale, interstate layer; the [[PUCO]] governs retail utility service inside Ohio;
and the [[Ohio Power Siting Board]] certifies where *major* energy facilities are
sited. A
hyperscale project can touch all three, and knowing which body owns which decision is
how the platform locates the right docket for a given question about power supply.

title: FFA
summary: A CERCLA cleanup agreement between EPA and a federal facility that sets the enforceable schedule and terms for remediating a listed site.
body:
A **federal facility agreement** is the enforceable compact between the [[EPA]] (often
with the state) and a federal installation on the Superfund National Priorities List.
Under CERCLA §120, a federal agency running a listed facility must enter such an
agreement, and it is the instrument that binds the cleanup: it fixes the schedule,
the milestones, and the interagency oversight for remediating the site's
contamination under [[CERCLA]].

For a record that touches a military or other federal installation, the FFA is the
backbone document of the environmental story. It establishes what contamination was
found, what the responsible agency committed to do about it, and on what timeline —
turning a diffuse cleanup into a set of dated, [verified] obligations the platform can
track and hold the facility to.

title: Grant-refund clause
summary: RDA §5.5 — public grant awards (State 629 / ODOD Jobs & Commerce) can backfill and refund the developer's "private" road-work contribution, dollar for dollar.
body:
The **grant-refund clause** is §5.5 of the [[roadwork development agreement]],
titled the "Overpayment Amount." It provides that if the road-work project
receives public grant awards — Ohio's State 629 funds or ODOD Jobs & Commerce
grants — that public money effectively backfills the developer's "Company
Contribution," and the corresponding amount is refunded to the Company.

The mechanism qualifies the claim that the $14.5M road package is *privately*
funded: to the extent public grants are awarded, public money can substitute for
the private contribution. The clause is read from the executed agreement; what
share of the contribution is ultimately refunded is not fixed in the document —
it depends on the grants actually awarded.

title: HB
summary: A bill originating in the Ohio House of Representatives, cited by number where it changes the siting, tax, or environmental law a project turns on.
body:
A **House Bill** is a legislative measure introduced in the Ohio House of
Representatives, referred to by number (HB 6, for example). Until enacted it is a
proposal; once passed by both chambers and signed, it amends the [[Ohio Revised Code]],
so a bill number is how a change in the law is tracked from introduction through its
codified result.

House bills matter to the record because the rules governing large projects are
actively being rewritten. Legislation reshaping utility and energy law, the siting
authority of the [[Ohio Power Siting Board]], or the property-tax tools behind a
data-center deal moves through numbered bills, often amid heavy lobbying. Following the
bill — its sponsors, its amendments, and the R.C. sections it alters — is how the
platform connects a statutory shift to the interests that pushed for it.

title: Heat reuse
summary: Capturing a data center's rejected thermal energy and redirecting it to on-site or district heating instead of dumping it — a cooling-design axis distinct from how much water the cooling draw consumes.
body:
**Heat reuse** is the design choice to *recover* a data center's rejected thermal
energy — piping it to on-site heating or a neighboring building / district-heat
loop — rather than *dumping* it through evaporative towers or dry coolers. It is a
third axis on the cooling-design space, orthogonal to the withdraw-vs-consume
question that [[consumptive cooling]] describes: a campus can dump or recover heat
at either end of the water-use band.

The axis matters here for two reasons. First, where recovery displaces evaporative
rejection it couples to the water story — less heat sent to a cooling tower is less
water evaporated. Second, closed-loop **chip cooling** (direct-to-chip liquid loops,
oil-free magnetic-bearing compressors) sits on the efficient, low-water pole and is
now a deployed hyperscale option, not just a spec sheet.

For a [[hyperscale data center]] the reuse choice is a disclosed-design fact, not
something the footprint reveals. It is treated here as an **industry reference**
design lever — bounding the space of what a campus *could* do — and never as a claim
about any watershed point's cooling design, which stays `[open]` until the operator
discloses it. The named-vendor examples (Danfoss heat-reuse modules and Turbocor
compressors in Google data centers) rest on a single promotional source — the
Danfoss–Google strategic-partnership announcement (Jan 2024), catalogued as
`[reference]` in the `heat_reuse` prior of
`data/reference/datacenter-industry/priors.yaml` (which carries the release URL):
it establishes that the technology is real and deployed, not that any particular
campus uses it.

title: HSG
summary: The NRCS A–D classification of a soil by how readily it infiltrates water — a primary input to runoff curve-number modeling.
body:
A **hydrologic soil group** sorts a soil into one of four classes — A, B, C, or D —
by its infiltration rate when thoroughly wet. Group A soils (sand, gravel) soak up
rain and shed little runoff; group D soils (clay, shallow-to-bedrock) infiltrate
poorly and run off fast. The classification comes from the NRCS soil survey.

HSG is the soil half of the runoff calculation: paired with land cover it fixes the
[[curve number]] that sets how much of a storm becomes runoff. It matters twice for
a development record. It decides how sensitive a site is to the impervious cover a
data-center campus adds, and — because the group can shift between survey editions —
choosing the wrong HSG (say C instead of B) silently changes the modeled runoff, a
drift the platform pins by sourcing the group explicitly rather than defaulting it.

title: HUC
summary: The USGS nested numeric code that keys a hydrologic area at a chosen scale, from large subbasins (HUC-8) down to local subwatersheds (HUC-12).
body:
A **hydrologic unit code** is the [[USGS]] spatial key for a hydrologic drainage
area. The codes nest by scale: each added pair of digits subdivides the area, so a
HUC-8 identifies a subbasin (the working unit for a [[total maximum daily load]]) and
a HUC-12 a much smaller local subwatershed.

The HUC is the join key for hydrology in this record. It is how a facility's outfall
is tied to the impaired water it discharges to, how [[NWIS]] gauges and nutrient
loads are rolled up to a consistent drainage area, and how a watershed model like
[[SWAT]] is bounded. Getting the HUC right is what keeps a downstream analysis
anchored to the actual receiving system rather than a nearby but hydrologically
separate one.

title: Hyperscale data center
summary: A very large, cloud-scale data center campus; the local zoning code defines the term and gates it as a conditional use.
body:
A **hyperscale data center** is a data center built and operated at cloud scale —
typically multiple large halls on a single campus, with substantial electrical
and cooling infrastructure. The term is not just colloquial here: the American
Township zoning resolution defines *Data Center / Hyperscale Data Center* and
treats it as a conditional use in its industrial district.

The land-use footprint is what ties the term to the rest of this record — the
parcels assembled for the campus, the conditional-use application, and the
[[consumptive cooling]] draw the cooling infrastructure implies. Who controls the
assembling entities is a separate question, read through
[[common-control plumbing]] rather than asserted.

title: Hyperscaler
summary: A cloud operator that builds and runs data centers at massive scale — the class of companies (AWS, Microsoft, Google, Meta) behind most large campus projects.
body:
A **hyperscaler** is one of the handful of companies that operate cloud and computing
infrastructure at the largest scale — Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and Meta foremost among
them. They design, own, and run their [[hyperscale data center]] campuses directly, as
opposed to renting capacity in a multi-tenant [[colocation]] facility.

The hyperscaler is the actor at the center of the siting story, and usually the hardest
to see. Behind a code-named LLC and a [[non-disclosure agreement]], the same few
operators are driving the land options, the power demand that fills the
[[interconnection queue]] or forces [[behind-the-meter]] generation, and the water draw
a community is asked to accommodate. Identifying which hyperscaler stands behind a
project — from its power profile, its secure-tier requirements, its known expansion
pattern — is often the pivotal [inference] the platform works to establish and then
confirm.

title: IL6
summary: The U.S. Department of Defense cloud security classification for classified (SECRET-level) workloads — the tier that dictates a data center's physical and personnel controls.
body:
**Impact Level 6** is the highest tier in the Department of Defense's cloud security
model, authorizing workloads classified up to SECRET. Reaching it requires a facility
and its staff to meet stringent controls — physical separation, cleared personnel,
accreditation — well beyond a commercial data center's baseline.

IL6 is a signal in the siting record because it narrows who a facility can be for.
A campus built or accredited to IL6 is serving a government-secure mission, which
constrains the operator, the tenants, and often the secrecy around it — a stronger
confidentiality posture than a commercial [[hyperscale data center]] or a multi-tenant
[[colocation]] site. Where the record hints at an IL6 requirement, the platform treats
it as a lead about the customer and the purpose, held as an [inference] until an
accreditation or contract document confirms it.

title: Interconnection queue
summary: The backlog of proposed generators and large loads awaiting the grid-connection studies and approvals an RTO requires before they can energize.
body:
The **interconnection queue** is the ordered backlog of projects — new generators and,
increasingly, large loads like data centers — waiting for the [[regional transmission
organization]] to study their effect on the grid and approve their connection. Each
entrant holds a dated queue position, and its studies determine what network upgrades
it must fund before it can energize.

The queue is one of the most reliable early indicators of a hyperscale project. A
campus that has said nothing publicly may already sit in [[PJM]]'s queue with a load
figure and a point of interconnection attached, and the studies expose the upgrade
cost and timeline the local grid faces. A long queue or a costly upgrade is also what
pushes an operator toward [[behind-the-meter]] generation to sidestep the wait — so
the queue shapes not just *when* a project connects but *how* it chooses to power
itself.

title: JEDD
summary: An Ohio township–municipality compact (R.C. 715.70) that shares income-tax revenue from a development area without annexation.
body:
A **joint economic development district** is an Ohio compact under R.C. 715.70 in
which a township and a municipality jointly govern a development area and share the
income-tax revenue it generates. It lets a township host commercial development —
which townships otherwise cannot tax on income — by borrowing a city's taxing
authority, in exchange for city services or a revenue split, and without the parcel
being annexed.

The JEDD matters to a large project because it decides *who* collects the payroll tax
a campus generates and *who* has a governance seat over it. A data-center JEDD can
route income-tax revenue across jurisdictional lines and bundle in the same
[[tax abatement]] and [[community reinvestment area]] terms as a straight municipal
deal. Because a JEDD is a negotiated multi-party contract, its text is often where the
real allocation of a project's benefits and obligations is written down.

title: Moratorium
summary: A temporary local ban on approving a class of development while a government reconsiders the rules that govern it.
body:
A **moratorium** is a time-limited pause a local government imposes on accepting or
approving a category of development — commonly while it drafts or revises zoning to
catch up with a pressure it did not anticipate. It freezes the status quo so
applications cannot vest under rules the community has decided to change.

In this record the moratorium is a recurring civic response to data-center demand: a
township or city facing a rush of large-load proposals halts approvals to write siting
standards, buffer or water rules, or an outright district. A moratorium is a live
signal — it marks where a community is contesting a project rather than waving it
through — and its timing relative to a specific application often determines whether
that project proceeds under old rules or new ones. It typically travels with a
[[rezoning]] fight, since the rules being paused are the ones a rezoning would apply.

title: NDA
summary: A confidentiality agreement that binds a party to secrecy, often shielding the terms and identity behind a data-center deal during site selection.
body:
A **non-disclosure agreement** is a contract in which a party agrees not to reveal
specified information. In economic development it is the routine instrument by which a
[[hyperscaler]] keeps a project confidential during site selection — binding a city,
county, utility, or economic-development agency to secrecy about the company's identity,
the incentives under negotiation, and the load involved, often under a code name.

The NDA is where public accountability and private deal-making collide in this record.
A confidentiality agreement between a public body and a private developer can wall off
exactly the terms — the [[tax abatement]], the water and power commitments — that the
public has an interest in seeing, and its scope is frequently contested through
public-records law. An NDA cannot override a statutory records duty, so the tension
between a signed confidentiality clause and R.C. 149.43 is a recurring seam the
platform documents rather than accepts at face value.

title: NPDES
summary: The Clean Water Act permit program that sets and enforces pollutant limits on point-source discharges to surface water.
body:
The **National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System** is the Clean Water Act
program that licenses point-source discharges to waters of the United States. An
NPDES permit names the outfall and receiving water, caps each regulated pollutant
with numeric [[effluent]] limits, and sets the monitoring and reporting requirements
the permittee must meet — chiefly by filing the [[discharge monitoring report]].

In Ohio the program is delegated to the [[Ohio EPA]], which issues NPDES permits
under state authority; a new or expanded source also needs a [[permit to install]]
before construction. The permit's fact sheet is the platform's primary source for a
receiving water's design low flow (the [[7Q10]]) and the [[assimilative capacity]]
available to dilute a load — the same denominators that a large new
[[consumptive cooling]] withdrawal would draw down.

Where a receiving water is impaired, the permit's limits are meant to implement the
water body's [[total maximum daily load]] through a point-source
[[wasteload allocation]]. Compliance history — inspections, violations, and any
[[significant non-compliance]] flag — is public through EPA's [[ECHO]].

title: NWIS
summary: The USGS system that serves real-time and historical streamflow and water-quality data from the national gauge network.
body:
The **National Water Information System** is the [[USGS]] database and web service
behind the nation's streamgages. It publishes discharge (flow) and stage, plus water
temperature and quality where instrumented, as both a live feed and a long historical
record, each gauge addressed by a site number.

NWIS is the live-flow spine of the water balance. The platform's hydrology
connectors pull gauge records from NWIS to establish a reach's actual flow regime,
and the long record is what a design low flow like the [[7Q10]] is computed from.
Reading flow from a real, dated NWIS gauge — rather than estimating it — is what lets
a receiving-water value be tagged [verified] and joined by [[HUC]] to the facility
under study.

title: OEPA
summary: The Ohio Environmental Protection Agency — the state permitting and enforcement authority for water, air, and waste under delegated federal programs.
body:
The **Ohio Environmental Protection Agency** is the state agency that carries out most
environmental permitting and enforcement in Ohio under authority delegated by the
federal [[EPA]]. It issues the [[NPDES]] water-discharge permits, the
[[permit to install]] that precedes construction, and the air permits a facility
operates under, and it brings the enforcement actions when those permits are violated.

For this record the Ohio EPA is the agency whose files carry the operative facts about
a facility's water and air impact — the permit terms, the fact sheets, the compliance
history. It is also the agency a public-records request most often targets, and where
the tension between disclosure and a company's confidentiality claims plays out. Its
decisions sit alongside those of the [[Ohio Power Siting Board]] on the energy side and
the federal EPA above it.

title: Once-through cooling
summary: A cooling design that withdraws water, passes it once to absorb heat, and returns nearly all of it to the source — warmer but not consumed.
body:
**Once-through cooling** draws water, runs it once through a heat exchanger, and
returns almost all of it to the source. Its signature is a large *withdrawal* but a
small *consumption*: the water comes back, chiefly warmer. The environmental question
it raises is thermal — the heat load and intake entrainment — rather than lost flow.

It is the mirror image of [[closed-loop cooling]], and the distinction is decisive
for the water balance. A once-through data center barely dents downstream flow but
adds a thermal load a receiving water may not tolerate at low flow; a recirculating
one withdraws far less yet consumes most of what it takes through evaporation. Which
design an operator chooses therefore determines whether a campus reads as a
[[consumptive cooling]] problem or a thermal one — so the platform keeps the cooling
type an explicit, sourced assumption, not a guess.

title: OPC
summary: A design-phase cost estimate for a public project — the engineer's structured projection of what construction will cost, and the artifact this platform reconstructs from source PDFs.
body:
An **opinion of probable cost** is the design engineer's structured estimate of what a
public project will cost to build, prepared before bids come in. It rolls up quantities
and unit prices into sections and subtotals, then adds markups for contingency and soft
costs — a document precise enough to budget against but explicitly an *opinion*, not a
bid.

The OPC is the reference artifact of the platform's extract stage: the six Tetra Tech
roundabout estimates it reconstructs from a scanned bundle are OPCs, and the
extraction model is built to hold any contractor's section-and-markup structure
without hardcoding one firm's taxonomy. Because the OCR text layer of a scanned OPC
garbles digits, its figures are read from the page image, and each extracted value
carries its page provenance — a dollar total is [verified] from the sheet, an
uncertain quantity marked approximate. It is the cost counterpart to how a project is
procured, whether by [[construction manager at risk]] or competitive bid.

title: OPSB
summary: The Ohio board that reviews and certifies the siting of major electric generation and transmission facilities.
body:
The **Ohio Power Siting Board** is the state body that must certify major energy
infrastructure — large generating plants, high-voltage transmission lines, and big
substations — before they are built. Its review weighs need, environmental impact,
and public comment through an evidentiary case docketed under a case number, which
makes the OPSB file a rich public record of a project's rationale and opposition.

For the data-center thread the OPSB is often where the *power* side of a campus first
surfaces publicly. A new substation or a behind-the-meter generation plant sized to a
hyperscale load lands on the board's docket, and the filing can reveal the load —
and the operator — before any economic-development announcement does. The board is
distinct from the [[PUCO]], which regulates utility service and rates, and from the
federal [[FERC]]; the OPSB decides *where* big energy facilities go.

title: ORC
summary: The codified statutes of Ohio, cited throughout the record — from public-records law to the economic-development and siting authorities.
body:
The **Ohio Revised Code** is the compiled, numbered body of Ohio's statutes, cited in
the form *R.C. 149.43* (or ORC 149.43). It is the legal backbone of the record: nearly
every authority a party invokes — an agency's duty, a tool it uses, a right the
requester asserts — traces to a specific section of the code.

The same citations recur across the platform's threads. R.C. 149.43 is the Public
Records Act behind a [[constructive denial]] and a [[public-records mandamus]];
R.C. 3735 authorizes the [[community reinvestment area]]; R.C. 715.70 the
[[joint economic development district]]; R.C. 6111 the state water-pollution program.
A section number changes only when the legislature amends it through a
[[House Bill]] — so pinning a claim to its exact R.C. citation is how the platform ties
an action to the precise authority in force when it was taken.

title: PFAS
summary: A large class of persistent synthetic fluorinated compounds, increasingly regulated in drinking water, effluent, and biosolids.
body:
**Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances** are a class of thousands of synthetic
compounds built around highly stable carbon–fluorine bonds. That stability is why
they are called *forever chemicals*: they resist breakdown, accumulate in water and
tissue, and are mobile in groundwater. EPA has set enforceable drinking-water limits
for several PFAS and is phasing them into discharge monitoring and cleanup programs.

PFAS cut across several threads of this record. They appear as a drinking-water and
[[NPDES]] concern where a discharge or biosolids land application is a pathway; as a
[[CERCLA]] liability now that two PFAS (PFOA and PFOS) were designated hazardous
substances as of EPA's 2024 final rule; and as
reported releases in EPA's [[TRI]]. Because the regulatory picture is still moving,
the platform tags a specific PFAS finding to its dated source — a [verified] limit or
a [reference] sampling result — rather than to a general expectation.

title: PILOT
summary: A negotiated payment that substitutes for the property taxes abated on a development, often directed to specific recipients like a school district.
body:
A **payment in lieu of taxes** is money a developer agrees to pay in place of the
property taxes a [[tax abatement]] has exempted. Because an abatement can strip most
of a project's value off the tax rolls, a PILOT is how the affected jurisdictions —
especially the school district, which depends on property tax — recover part of what
they would otherwise have collected.

The PILOT is where the real fiscal bargain of an abated deal lives. Its size relative
to the taxes forgone, and who receives it, determine whether an abatement is roughly
revenue-neutral for schools or a large net transfer to the developer. A
[[tax increment financing]] service payment is a close structural cousin — both
convert a tax obligation into a directed payment. The platform reads the PILOT terms
next to the abatement they offset, because one number without the other overstates
the public benefit.

title: PJM
summary: The regional transmission organization that operates the high-voltage grid and wholesale electricity market across Ohio and the mid-Atlantic.
body:
**PJM Interconnection** is the [[regional transmission organization]] that runs the
transmission grid and the wholesale power market for Ohio and all or parts of a dozen
neighboring states plus the District of Columbia. It dispatches generation, runs the capacity market, and — critically for this
record — administers the [[interconnection queue]] that every new generator or large
load must clear before it can connect.

PJM is where a data center's grid impact becomes visible at regional scale. Its
queue, capacity-auction results, and load forecasts document the demand that
hyperscale campuses are placing on the system, often earlier and more concretely than
any local filing. As a federally regulated market operator PJM answers to [[FERC]],
while the physical facilities it interconnects are sited through state bodies like the
[[Ohio Power Siting Board]] — so a single project leaves a trail across all three.

title: POTW
summary: The Clean Water Act term for a municipally owned wastewater treatment works — the public peer of a private industrial discharger.
body:
A **publicly owned treatment works** is the Clean Water Act's name for a
municipally owned [[WWTP]] and its collection system. The label matters because a
POTW carries obligations a private plant does not: it must administer a
*pretreatment* program that limits what industrial users may send to the sewer, and
it discharges its own treated [[effluent]] under a municipal [[NPDES]] permit.

For the platform, the POTW distinction sorts a discharger by who runs it. A
hyperscale campus that routes cooling blowdown or sanitary flow to the local POTW
becomes an industrial user inside that public permit *for that stream* rather than a
permittee in its own right — which changes where the monitoring record lives and who
is accountable for an exceedance. Any separate direct discharge, stormwater, or other
regulated source at the same campus can still require its own facility-specific
permit.

title: PTI
summary: Ohio EPA's pre-construction permit for a new or modified source of air or water pollution, issued before ground is broken.
body:
A **permit to install** is the [[Ohio EPA]] authorization a project must obtain
*before* it builds or modifies a source of pollution — a treatment unit, an outfall,
an air-emitting process. It is the pre-construction counterpart to an operating
permit: the PTI reviews the design, while an operating permit governs the source once
it runs — where applicable an [[NPDES]] permit for a water discharge, and for air a
Title V permit for a major source or a permit-to-install-and-operate (PTIO) for a
smaller one.

The PTI is often the earliest hard document in a facility's public trail, because it
predates operation. For a data-center campus, a permit-to-install application can
surface the on-site combustion, backup generation, or wastewater handling before the
operator has said anything publicly — which is why the platform treats a PTI as a
high-value discovery target alongside the [[construction general permit]] that covers
its stormwater during the build.

title: Public-records mandamus
summary: In Ohio, a writ of mandamus is the remedy that compels a public office to produce records improperly withheld under the Public Records Act.
body:
A **public-records request (PRR)** asks a public office to produce records under
Ohio's Public Records Act (R.C. 149.43). When an office withholds or fails to
produce responsive records, the statutory remedy is a writ of **mandamus** — a
court order compelling production (and, in some cases, statutory damages).

The mandamus thread is the lever that pries loose otherwise withheld material:
the withholding map, the source instruments, and the production analyses sit
under the legal-history section. The records it produced are what the structured
extractions and the entity graph are built on — which is why the
[[common-control plumbing]] read from them is only as complete as the
production was.

title: PUCO
summary: Ohio's utility regulator, overseeing the rates and service of electric, gas, water, and telecom utilities in the state.
body:
The **Public Utilities Commission of Ohio** regulates the state's investor-owned
utilities — setting the rates, terms, and service standards under which a company
like [[AEP]] Ohio delivers electricity. Its cases run as docketed proceedings with
filed testimony and public comment, so a PUCO docket is a durable record of what a
utility proposed and what it was allowed.

PUCO is where the *cost* of accommodating a new large load can surface: a utility's
request to build infrastructure, recover a special-contract arrangement, or shift the
cost of serving a hyperscale customer onto or away from other ratepayers runs through
the commission. It pairs with the [[Ohio Power Siting Board]], which certifies where a
major facility is built; the separate federal [[FERC]] holds jurisdiction over
interstate wholesale power, while the PUCO's own authority is the state's retail
service and rates — a division of labor the platform keeps straight when
tracing who approved what.

title: PUE
summary: A data center's total facility energy divided by its IT-load energy — the standard measure of how much overhead (mostly cooling) its computing carries.
body:
**Power usage effectiveness** is the ratio of a data center's total energy use to the
energy delivered to its IT equipment. A PUE of 1.0 would mean every watt reached the
servers; real facilities land above that, and the gap is overhead — chiefly cooling and
power conversion. A modern efficient campus reports a PUE near 1.1–1.2.

PUE is the lever that connects computing to cooling, and through cooling to water. A
lower PUE means less energy spent moving heat, but the efficient designs that achieve
it often lean on evaporative [[consumptive cooling]], trading electricity for water —
which is why PUE and its water counterpart, [[WUE]], have to be read together. The
platform treats an operator's reported PUE as a claimed [reference] figure, useful for
scaling a [[hyperscale data center]]'s total draw from its IT load but not a
substitute for the actual metered demand.

title: Rezoning
summary: A legislative change to a parcel's zoning district, frequently the approval that unlocks — or blocks — a large project.
body:
A **rezoning** is a legislative act that changes the zoning classification of a
parcel — an industrial district applied to former farmland, say — so a use the old
zoning barred becomes permitted. Because it is legislative, it is usually decided by
the elected body after a planning-commission recommendation and public hearing, and it
is the approval most exposed to organized opposition and, in some jurisdictions, to
referendum.

Rezoning is usually the hinge in a data-center land record: the campus needs
industrial or a special district, and the vote to grant it is where a community's
position becomes official and, depending on the jurisdiction, open to referendum or
judicial challenge. It is distinct from the lesser approvals a
project might instead seek — a [[conditional use]] permit within the existing zoning,
or a [[variance]] from a single standard — and it is the approval a
[[moratorium]] most often pauses. Tracking the rezoning vote, its conditions, and any
referendum is how the platform fixes when and on what terms a project was actually
authorized.

title: RFP
summary: A solicitation asking firms to submit a scoped, priced proposal, evaluated on a combination of approach and cost.
body:
A **request for proposals** is a public solicitation that asks firms for a complete,
scoped, and priced offer to do the work. Unlike a pure low-bid invitation, an RFP is
scored on stated criteria — technical approach, schedule, team, and price together — so
the agency can select the best value rather than merely the cheapest number.

For the platform, an RFP and the proposals it draws are a rich seam of the public
record: they lay out how a project was defined, who competed, and what each offered.
An RFP typically follows a [[request for qualifications]] when an agency first
shortlists on competence and then seeks priced proposals from the shortlist, and its
figures can be read against the design-phase [[opinion of probable cost]] to see how
bid reality tracked the engineer's estimate.

title: RFQ
summary: A solicitation asking firms to submit their qualifications, used to shortlist or select on competence rather than price.
body:
A **request for qualifications** is a public solicitation that asks interested firms to
document their experience, staffing, and capacity — their *qualifications* — rather than
a price. An agency uses it to shortlist candidates before a priced proposal, or, for
professional and qualifications-based services, to select outright and negotiate the fee
afterward.

The RFQ is the front door to a project's procurement record and often names the field of
competitors before anyone is chosen. It is the customary selection route for a
[[construction manager at risk]] and for design engineers, where qualifications rather
than low bid govern. It pairs with the [[request for proposals]], which does ask for a
scoped, priced offer — together they mark how and on what basis a public project's team
was assembled.

title: Roadwork Development Agreement
summary: The agreement under which the developer funds the public road work around the campus — a ~$14.5M "Company Contribution" set against the $14.2M cost estimate, with clauses on grant-refunds, records-notice, and procurement.
body:
The **Roadwork Development Agreement** (RDA) is the contract under which the
data-center developer agrees to fund the public road work around the campus —
four roundabouts and two corridor rebuilds — while the County and Port Authority
take those roads into public maintenance in perpetuity. Allen County Resolution
#588-25 adopted it, effective 2025-09-15.

Its headline is a private gift: a "Company Contribution" of **$14,500,000**, set
against the Tetra Tech Opinion of Probable Cost of $14,223,081. Three clauses
complicate the word *private*, each read from the executed agreement:

- **§5.5** (the "Overpayment Amount") lets public grant awards — State 629 and
  ODOD Jobs & Commerce grants — backfill and refund the contribution to the
  Company; see the [[grant-refund clause]].
- **§9.13** requires the Authority to give the Company at least five business
  days' notice before releasing the agreement in response to a records request.
- **§9.17** exempts the Company from any competitive procurement for the work.

The RDA is one of the instruments examined in the records-withholding analysis
([[public-records-mandamus]]), where §9.13 sits alongside the NDA and CRA as a
developer-notice clause. What the clauses say is read from the document; the
characterization of the layers as a designed system is argument, labelled as such.

title: RSEI
summary: EPA's model that converts Toxics Release Inventory reports into a comparative, toxicity- and exposure-weighted chronic-risk score.
body:
**Risk-Screening Environmental Indicators** is the [[EPA]] model that turns the raw
pounds in the [[TRI]] into a comparative risk score. It weights each reported release
by the chemical's toxicity and models how it disperses and reaches people, so a small
release of a potent compound near a population can outrank a large release of a benign
one far from anyone.

RSEI is a *screening* tool, not a measurement of harm to any individual — its value is
in ranking and trend, letting an analyst compare facilities and watch a site's risk
profile move over time. The platform pulls RSEI as a committed [reference] dataset
scoped to a site's geography, and treats a score as an [inference] about relative
chronic risk rather than a [verified] exposure. Its inputs are only as current as the
TRI year it was run on.

title: RTO
summary: The independent operator that runs the transmission grid and wholesale energy market for a multi-state region — PJM in this record.
body:
A **regional transmission organization** is an independent, FERC-regulated entity
that operates the high-voltage grid and wholesale electricity market for a region,
keeping the transmission system neutral among the utilities and generators that use
it. An *independent system operator* (ISO) is the functionally equivalent term; the
label differs by region but the role is the same.

The RTO is the level at which grid capacity is actually allocated, through the
[[interconnection queue]] and capacity market it administers. For this record the RTO
is [[PJM]], and its rules — set under [[FERC]] tariffs — determine how quickly a new
hyperscale load or a behind-the-meter plant can connect, and what it must pay to do
so. Understanding the RTO's process is what turns a vague "grid constraint" into a
specific, dated position in a queue.

title: SNC
summary: EPA's flag for a permittee whose violations are serious or chronic enough to warrant a formal enforcement response.
body:
**Significant non-compliance** is EPA's threshold for a permit violation serious
enough to demand a formal response rather than a routine notice. For a water
permittee it is triggered by patterns in the [[discharge monitoring report]] —
effluent exceedances above defined magnitudes, or chronic reporting failures — not
by a single stray value.

An SNC flag is a signal worth following: it marks the facilities EPA itself has
sorted as problem dischargers, and it is visible through [[ECHO]] without any
records request. An unresolved SNC is frequently the on-ramp to a formal enforcement
action and, ultimately, a [[consent decree]]. The platform reads an SNC designation
as [verified] when it appears in the ECHO record, and treats the underlying cause as
a lead to trace back through the [[NPDES]] permit and its monitoring history.

title: SOS
summary: The state office that holds business-entity filings — the public trail from an LLC back toward the people and companies behind it.
body:
The **Secretary of State** is the state office that registers business entities and
keeps their public filings — articles of organization, statutory agents, annual
reports, and the record of mergers and name changes. For an investigator it is the
entry point of corporate genealogy: the place a limited-liability company's paper trail
begins.

The SOS record is central to the entity work in this platform because data-center
developers routinely route a project through single-purpose LLCs with anodyne names.
Chasing the filings — the registered agent shared across shells, the formation date
that lines up with a land option, the parent disclosed in an out-of-state filing — is
how the platform pierces a code name toward the operator behind it. The trail is often
partial by design, which is where a [[non-disclosure agreement]] and other
confidentiality layers pick up where the public filing goes quiet.

title: SSA
summary: An EPA designation for an aquifer that supplies most of the drinking water for an area with no readily available alternative source.
body:
A **sole source aquifer** is an aquifer that the [[EPA]] has designated as the
principal drinking-water source for its service area — one supplying at least half
the area's drinking water with no economically feasible alternative if it were
contaminated. The designation does not create a cleanup program, but it triggers EPA
review of federally funded projects that could contaminate the aquifer.

The label raises the stakes of any subsurface contamination in the designated area:
a release that would be a local matter over a redundant aquifer becomes a threat to
the region's only water supply. Where a sole-source aquifer underlies a facility
already inside a federal cleanup — a [[CERCLA]] site — the two designations
compound, and the groundwater pathway becomes the controlling exposure route in the
record.

title: SWAT
summary: A watershed-scale model that simulates runoff, sediment, and nutrient loading across a basin to support TMDL and land-use analysis.
body:
The **Soil and Water Assessment Tool** is a watershed model that routes rainfall
through a basin's soils, land cover, and channels to estimate runoff, sediment, and
nutrient loads over time. It works at the [[HUC]] scale, dividing a basin into
subwatersheds so land-use change in one area can be traced to loading downstream.

SWAT is the kind of model that stands behind a nutrient [[total maximum daily load]]:
it apportions a reach's [[total phosphorus]] and nitrogen load among its sources,
which is what a load budget and its allocations are built on. The platform treats a
SWAT output as a modeled [inference] — useful for attributing and comparing loads,
but distinct from a measured [[discharge monitoring report]] value, and only as good
as the land-cover and soil inputs it was run on.

title: SWCD
summary: A local district that administers soil, drainage, and stormwater conservation programs, often reviewing the erosion controls on new development.
body:
A **soil and water conservation district** is a local governmental unit — typically
county-based — that carries out soil, drainage, and stormwater conservation work. Its
roots are agricultural, but on the development side it frequently reviews grading and
drainage plans and — where a local MS4 program, ordinance, or delegation agreement
provides for it — inspects the [[erosion and sediment control]] a construction site
must maintain under its [[construction general permit]]. Formal enforcement of the
permit itself stays with the regulator, not the district.

The SWCD is the local eyes on a large construction disturbance. Where the [[Ohio EPA]]
holds the discharge permit, the district is often the body that actually walks the site
and flags a sediment-control failure, and its records can document a project's
compliance — or its lapses — during the build. For a multi-hundred-acre data-center
clearing, the district's review and inspection file is a ground-level source the
platform mines for what actually happened on the dirt.

title: Tax abatement
summary: A negotiated reduction or exemption of property taxes granted to attract or retain development — the umbrella over Ohio's CRA, enterprise-zone, and TIF tools.
body:
A **tax abatement** is a negotiated agreement to forgive some or all of the property
taxes a development would otherwise owe, granted to induce the investment. In Ohio it
is delivered through named vehicles — a [[community reinvestment area]], an
[[enterprise zone]], or a [[tax increment financing]] district — each with its own
statute, term limits, and approval path, but all resting on the same trade: public
revenue given up now for private investment and jobs later.

Abatement is the fiscal core of the data-center siting story, because the projects
are enormous in assessed value but modest in permanent employment, so the value
exempted can dwarf the payroll returned. Reading a deal honestly means netting the
abatement against what offsets it — a [[payment in lieu of taxes]], a school
revenue-share, a grant-refund clause that lets the public recover if promises
fail — rather than citing the headline investment alone. That netting is how the
platform tests a claimed public benefit against its documented public cost.

title: TIF
summary: A financing tool that earmarks the property-tax increment from new development to pay for public infrastructure serving it.
body:
**Tax increment financing** freezes the taxable value of a parcel or district at its
pre-development level and diverts the *increment* — the added taxes owed on the new
value — to pay for public improvements that serve the development, often through
payments the owner makes in lieu of the diverted taxes. Ohio structures a TIF as an
exemption paired with a service payment, so mechanically it resembles a
[[tax abatement]] with the savings recycled into infrastructure.

TIF is the tool that funds the roads, water, and sewer a large campus needs without a
general tax increase, by capturing the project's own future tax growth up front. In a
data-center deal it frequently rides alongside a [[community reinvestment area]]
abatement — the CRA exempts the building value while the TIF finances the offsite
infrastructure. Untangling which mechanism captures which value, and for how long, is
what separates a project's advertised investment from its net fiscal effect.

title: TMDL
summary: The maximum pollutant load an impaired water body can receive and still meet water-quality standards, apportioned among the sources that contribute it.
body:
A **total maximum daily load** is the pollutant budget for an impaired water body:
the maximum daily load of a given pollutant the water can absorb and still meet its
water-quality standard, plus a margin of safety. The Clean Water Act requires a
state to write one for each impaired water body–pollutant combination on its list.

The budget is then divided. Point sources — permitted dischargers — receive a
[[wasteload allocation]], which a state implements by writing that share into each
facility's [[NPDES]] permit; nonpoint sources (runoff) receive a load allocation.
In this watershed the binding TMDLs are nutrient budgets for
[[total phosphorus]] and [[total nitrogen]], the loads that drive the Lake
Erie / Maumee algae problem. A TMDL tightens the [[dilution]] math: it can leave a
reach with little or no headroom for a new load, regardless of that reach's flow.

title: Total nitrogen
summary: A nutrient water-quality parameter summing the nitrogen species in a sample, tracked alongside phosphorus in loading and TMDL analysis.
body:
**Total nitrogen** is a reporting aggregate of a sample's nitrogen forms — derived,
depending on what a lab measures, either as a direct TN result or by summing nitrate,
nitrite, ammonia, and organic nitrogen (often via total Kjeldahl nitrogen plus nitrate
and nitrite). Like [[total phosphorus]], it is a nutrient that
fuels algal growth; while phosphorus usually limits freshwater blooms, nitrogen
co-drives them and governs the toxicity of some cyanobacteria, so a nutrient
[[total maximum daily load]] typically tracks both.

Nitrogen also matters directly to permit compliance: ammonia is toxic to aquatic
life at low concentrations and its decay consumes oxygen, so a discharge's nitrogen
load ties straight into the receiving water's [[dissolved oxygen]] budget. The
platform reads total nitrogen as one of the two nutrient loads that decide whether a
reach can absorb a new discharge, not as a stand-alone number.

title: Total phosphorus
summary: A nutrient water-quality parameter measuring all forms of phosphorus in a sample; excess loading drives the Lake Erie / Maumee algal-bloom problem.
body:
**Total phosphorus** measures every form of phosphorus in a water sample —
dissolved and particulate — as a single number. Phosphorus is usually the limiting
nutrient for freshwater algae, so it is the parameter regulators watch most closely
in the Western Lake Erie basin, where phosphorus loading feeds the harmful algal
blooms that recur in the [[Maumee]] watershed.

Because it is the driver, total phosphorus is the pollutant most likely to carry a
binding [[total maximum daily load]] and a point-source [[wasteload allocation]] in
this record. A reach already over its phosphorus budget has no assimilative headroom
for a new load no matter how much water it carries — and the bloom itself worsens the
[[dissolved oxygen]] sag that stresses aquatic life downstream.

title: TRI
summary: EPA's annual, facility-level inventory of reported toxic-chemical releases to air, water, and land — the data behind the RSEI risk model.
body:
The **Toxics Release Inventory** is EPA's annual, self-reported accounting of toxic
chemicals released or transferred by industrial and federal facilities above
reporting thresholds. Each facility files quantities by chemical and medium — air,
water, land — creating a long, comparable public time series of who released what,
where.

TRI is a raw inventory of *pounds*, not of risk: a large release of a low-toxicity
chemical and a small release of a potent one look different on paper but not in
proximity to people. That gap is exactly what the [[RSEI]] model closes, weighting TRI
quantities by toxicity and population exposure. The platform uses TRI as the neutral,
[reference] baseline of a site's release profile, and watches the list expand as newly
regulated compounds like some [[PFAS]] are phased into reporting.

title: USGS
summary: The federal science agency that operates the national streamgage network and publishes the water, terrain, and geology data the analysis rests on.
body:
The **United States Geological Survey** is the federal earth-science agency. For this
record its role is water and terrain: it runs the streamgage network served through
[[NWIS]], defines the watershed addressing of the [[hydrologic unit code]], and
publishes the elevation and geologic layers that underpin drainage and siting work.

USGS data is authoritative reference in the platform's evidence grammar — a gauge
reading or a mapped watershed boundary is a [reference] fact from a neutral federal
source, not an agency's contested position. That neutrality is why a design low-flow
statistic like the [[7Q10]] — the one that applies varies with the pollutant,
receiving water, jurisdiction, and permit method — is anchored to the USGS record: it
lets the water-quality math start from ground the parties don't dispute.

title: Variance
summary: A parcel-specific waiver of a zoning standard granted by a board of zoning appeals when strict application would impose an undue hardship.
body:
A **variance** is a waiver from a specific zoning requirement — a setback, a height,
a lot-coverage limit — granted by a board of zoning appeals for one parcel because
strict application would create a practical difficulty or hardship peculiar to that
property. An *area* variance relaxes a dimensional standard; a *use* variance, rarer
and harder to win, permits a use the district otherwise bars.

A variance is the narrowest of the land-use approvals: it does not change the
district ([[rezoning]]) or authorize a listed use ([[conditional use]]), it just bends
one rule for one site. In a large-project record variances tend to be the tell in the
details — the setback or buffer a campus needed to have relaxed, the standard it could not
meet as-designed — and a stack of them can reveal how far a project departs from the
zoning the parcel was granted. (Note this is a zoning variance, distinct from an
NPDES water-quality variance, which is an unrelated permitting instrument.)

title: WLA
summary: The share of a TMDL assigned to point-source dischargers, translated into the effluent limits of their NPDES permits.
body:
A **wasteload allocation** is the portion of a [[total maximum daily load]] handed
to point sources — the permitted dischargers, as distinct from the *load allocation*
given to diffuse runoff. It is the mechanism that turns a watershed-scale pollutant
budget into an enforceable limit at a specific pipe.

A state implements a WLA by writing it into the discharger's [[NPDES]] permit as a
water-quality-based [[effluent]] limit. So a WLA is where the abstract budget
becomes concrete: it determines whether a plant on an impaired reach has any load
headroom to absorb growth, or whether a new industrial or municipal load forces an
offset somewhere else in the watershed. When a reach's WLAs are already fully
subscribed, an added discharge has nowhere to go on paper.

title: WUE
summary: A data center's water use per unit of IT energy — the cooling-water efficiency ratio; whether it counts withdrawal or consumption depends on how it is reported, so the basis has to be recorded before the number is used.
body:
**Water usage effectiveness** measures a data center's cooling-water use against the
energy delivered to its IT equipment, usually stated in liters per kilowatt-hour. It is
the water peer of [[PUE]]: where PUE captures energy overhead, WUE captures how much
water the cooling system uses to reject the resulting heat. The convention counts
on-site *consumption*, but a reported WUE may instead be built on *withdrawal* — a
distinct quantity — so the metric basis has to be recorded, not assumed.

WUE is the coefficient that turns a computing load into a cooling-water quantity, which
is why it is central to the water thread. An evaporative, [[closed-loop cooling]] design
posts a higher WUE — it spends water to save electricity — while an air-cooled or
[[once-through cooling]] design posts a lower one. Multiplying a facility's IT energy by
a WUE yields that water quantity on the metric's own basis; getting to the
[[consumptive cooling]] draw the water-balance model tests against a reach's low flow
takes a further, separately labeled withdrawal-to-consumption assumption when the WUE
is a withdrawal figure. Because operators report WUE inconsistently, the platform
carries it as a labeled scenario input, not a measured fact.

title: WWTP
summary: The plant that treats sewage and industrial wastewater before discharging treated effluent to a receiving water under an NPDES permit.
body:
A **wastewater treatment plant** collects, treats, and discharges a community's
sewage. A municipally owned plant is a [[POTW]] in Clean Water Act terms; some
operators brand a modernized plant a *water reclamation facility* (WRF) to signal
higher-grade treatment and reuse. Either way, its treated [[effluent]] leaves
through a permitted outfall governed by an [[NPDES]] permit and is logged in the
plant's monthly [[discharge monitoring report]].

A WWTP is a load *and* a dilution source in the water balance: it adds treated flow
to the receiving water, so its discharge is part of the low-flow denominator that a
new [[consumptive cooling]] withdrawal competes against. When a data-center or
industrial user is added upstream, the plant's headroom — hydraulic and permitted —
is one of the first constraints the record tests.
